Title: Assessing the implementation of user-centred design standards on assistive technology for persons with visual impairments: a systematic review
Authors: Luisa Maria Ortiz-Escobar; Mario Andres Chavarria; Klaus Schonenberger; Samia Hurst; Michael Ashley Stein; Anthony Mugeere; Minerva Rivas Velarde
Research area: User-centred design (UCD) practice in assistive technology
Problem addressed: Unclear whether AT for VI users is actually developed per UCD standards (ISO 9241-210).
Target population: 24 studies (2012-2022) of AT for persons with visual impairments.
Methodology: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42022307466); ScienceDirect, Scopus, PMC, WoS; 348 records -> 24 included; MMAT quality appraisal; thematic synthesis against ISO 9241-210's six principles.
Main findings: 87.5% of studies from high-income countries, none from low-income; only 5 cited ISO 9241-210/13407; 35.71% engaged users only at the end; 28.57% collected no empirical user data; only 2 described team composition; weak description of context of use.
Limitations: Four databases, four languages; small, non-probability samples in included studies.
Research gaps: Little evidence that UCD improves outcomes; near absence of low/middle-income contexts; weak early-stage user research.
Relevance to SPARSH: Justifies SPARSH's explicit UCD process in an Indian (LMIC) setting and early involvement of caregivers and blind users.
Design implications: Document context of use (Indian modular switchboards, shared homes); engage users early, not only at final testing; report team composition and ISO 9241-210 alignment.

Title: SUS: A 'Quick and Dirty' Usability Scale
Journal/conference: In Usability Evaluation in Industry (Taylor & Francis); editors and pages not verified (commonly cited pp. 189-194)
Problem addressed: Need for a quick, low-cost global usability measure.
Methodology: 10-item, 5-point Likert questionnaire; items chosen by Likert technique.
Main findings: SUS presented as a reliable, low-cost global usability scale.
Relevance to SPARSH: Standard post-task measure for the caregiver app.
Design implications: Administer SUS to caregivers after setup; interpret with Bangor et al. adjectives (L40).

Title: An Empirical Evaluation of the System Usability Scale
Authors: Aaron Bangor; Philip T. Kortum; James T. Miller
Problem addressed: Psychometric evidence and interpretation of SUS.

Title: Determining What Individual SUS Scores Mean: Adding an Adjective Rating Scale
Authors: Aaron Bangor; Philip Kortum; James Miller
Problem addressed: Practitioners need a meaning for individual SUS scores.
Methodology: Added a 7-point adjective item to SUS; correlation analysis.
Main findings: Adjective correlated with SUS r = 0.822; mean SUS by adjective: Poor 35.7, OK 50.9, Good 71.4, Excellent 85.5, Best Imaginable 90.9; mean study score ~70.
Limitations: Endpoint categories had few data; 'OK' ambiguous.
Relevance to SPARSH: Lets SPARSH report SUS with interpretable labels.

Title: Development of NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): Results of Empirical and Theoretical Research
Authors: Sandra G. Hart; Lowell E. Staveland
Journal/conference: In P. A. Hancock & N. Meshkati (Eds.), Human Mental Workload (Advances in Psychology, Vol. 52, pp. 139-183). North-Holland
Problem addressed: Need a sensitive, reliable subjective workload measure.
Methodology: Analysis of subjective ratings of 10 factors across 16 experiments; derivation of a multi-dimensional scale combining six factors.
Main findings: Workload correlates varied with task, workload source and individual definitions; proposed six-factor scale.
Relevance to SPARSH: Measure caregiver workload during setup and blind-user workload when learning caps.
Design implications: Use raw TLX (unweighted) for brevity; administer orally/accessibly to blind participants.

Title: Representing Users in Accessibility Research
Problem addressed: Accessibility studies often fail to involve representative users.
Main findings: The field must raise standards for conducting and reporting accessibility research with representative users.
Relevance to SPARSH: Core citation for why SPARSH should not rely on blindfolded sighted participants.
Design implications: Recruit blind participants (e.g., via NAB/blind schools near Pilani or Delhi) and report their characteristics.

Title: Stumbling in Their Shoes: Disability Simulations Reduce Judged Capabilities of Disabled People
Authors: Arielle M. Silverman; Jason D. Gwinn; Leaf Van Boven
Journal/conference: Social Psychological and Personality Science, 6(4), 464-471 (online Nov 2014)
Target population: Participants in two experiments (n not verified).
Methodology: Two experiments comparing blindness simulation with other conditions.
Main findings: Simulating blindness led people to judge blind people as less capable of work and independent living; effect self-focused (simulators predicted they would cope poorly).
Relevance to SPARSH: Blindfolded sighted participants experience 'new blindness' and are not representative of experienced blind users' tactile skill or strategies.
Design implications: If blindfolded pilots are used, frame them as early functional checks only.

Title: Review of Quantitative Empirical Evaluations of Technology for People with Visual Impairments
Authors: Emeline Brule; Brianna J. Tomlinson; Oussama Metatla; Christophe Jouffrais; Marcos Serrano
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '20), pp. 1-14
Problem addressed: How VI technologies are evaluated quantitatively and with whom.
Target population: 178 papers (1988-2019; CHI, ASSETS, TOCHI, TACCESS), 243 evaluations.
Main findings: Median sample 12 (VI-only evaluations ~9.7); 14.4% of evaluations used blindfolded participants; sighted participants in 30% of experiments. Recommends sighted participants only for low-level interaction tests, validating final designs with VI people, reporting participant tables, single-subject designs for small populations.
Relevance to SPARSH: Gives SPARSH a defensible sample-size norm (~10 blind participants) and rules for when blindfolded pilots are acceptable.
Design implications: Use blindfolded sighted participants only for low-level discrimination pilots; validate cap recognition with blind participants; tabulate participant onset of blindness and braille literacy.

Title: Interdependence as a Frame for Assistive Technology Research and Design
Authors: Cynthia L. Bennett; Erin Brady; Stacy M. Branham
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 20th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '18), pp. 161-173
Methodology: Conceptual paper drawing on Disability Studies and authors' cases.
Main findings: Proposes interdependence - collaborative access and recognising contributions of disabled people - as a complementary (not prescriptive) frame.
Relevance to SPARSH: Frames SPARSH's caregiver-AI-blind user triad without positioning the blind user as passive.
Design implications: Let the blind user verify and correct caps (e.g., report a mislabeled switch) and request re-mapping.
